newsitem.title: FRANCE: Canal J launches first French childrens' news spot.
newsitem.headline: Canal J launches first French childrens' news spot.

text.p: French children's television channel Canal J said it is launching a daily news bulletin from the end of this month, the first such programme on French television.
Childrens' TV news bulletins have existed for some time in many European countries but have not so far taken off in France, a Canal J spokeswoman said on Tuesday.
France's terrestrial television channels tried out childrens' news bulletins 10 years ago but did not persevere with the experiment, she said.

She said Canal J was launching the childrens' news bulletin because of the popularity of its existing current affairs programme, which has been running for five years, and following a strong response to a poll it carried out asking children if they liked television news.
The bulletin will be broadcast at 1950 local time on weekdays, 10 minutes before the evening news on the main terrestrial channels, and at weekends, Canal J said in a statement.

It will deal with the three or four top news items of the day, and will also carry reports on subjects of special interest to children, like racketeering at school or the governments' promise of free school meals for the poorest children.

Canal J, created 12 years ago, has recently begun to face competition for its youthful audience from cartoon channel Teletoon and a French language version of Disney Channel, both now available on France's cable and satellite networks.
The Canal J spokeswoman said the competition did not seem to be hurting Canal J.
"There has been no slide in subscriptions. There is a steady rise every month," she said in answer to questions.
Canal J is broadcast on France's cable television networks and satellite service CanalSatellite. It had 1.87 million subscribers as at July 1 and has been in profit for two years.

It is owned 36.5 percent by Com-Dev Images, a unit of state-owned bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations (CDC), 32.5 percent by Lyonnaise Communications, a unit of Suez-Lyonnaise des Eaux, 19 percent by Canal Plus, six percent by magazine group Bayard Presse, 3.5 percent by Generale d'Images, a unit of Cie Generale des Eaux and 2.5 percent by magazine group Groupe Marie Claire.
